answer: db.run_no_throw returns a string, not Python objects — "[{A: Decimal(1,2)}]" is just a repr. literal_eval fails because Decimal(...) is not a literal. Fixes: (a) evaluate the repr with Decimal in scope: from decimal import Decimal; rows = eval(out, {"Decimal": Decimal}); or (b) better, execute the query directly (SQLAlchemy engine/cursor, or the SQLDatabase's underlying _execute) so you get a real list of dicts. pandas handles Decimal values fine once they are actual objects: df = pd.DataFrame(rows). Your one-character-per-cell CSV ("[ { A : D e...") happens because writer.writerows(out) iterates the string character by character — writerows expects an iterable of row sequences, not a string. Finally, give Streamlit the CSV text, not the open file handle: st.download_button(label="Download data as CSV", data=df.to_csv(index=False), file_name="filename.csv", mime="text/csv"). If you keep csv.writer, write header and df.itertuples() rows, then reopen the file (or seek(0) and read()) before passing its contents to download_button.

This is normal Docker behavior. Flask only sees the network interfaces inside the container's namespace: 127.0.0.1 (container loopback) and 172.17.0.2 (the container's address on Docker's default bridge network). It will never print the host's LAN IP (172.22.10.10) or a public IP — the container doesn't own those interfaces; traffic reaches it via port publishing/NAT. (a) Yes, you must run with -p 5000:5000. EXPOSE in the Dockerfile is metadata only; it does not publish anything. (b) Since Flask binds 0.0.0.0 inside the container, once the port is published you reach the app using the server's IP, e.g. http://172.22.10.10:5000 from the LAN, or the server's public IP if it has one and the firewall/security group opens port 5000. (c) 172.17.0.2 is reachable only from the Docker host itself. You'll never see a public IP listed unless an interface literally carries one; behind NAT only private addresses appear.

query alone can't express "up to the first time a condition occurs" because it filters rows independently. Build a boolean mask for the stop condition, then cut at its first occurrence with cummax (or idxmax). Example — keep rows until s01[m], s5.5[m] and s10[m] all exceed 10 for the first time:

stop = (df_GPS['s01[m]'] > 10) & (df_GPS['s5.5[m]'] > 10) & (df_GPS['s10[m]'] > 10)
subset = df_GPS[~stop.cummax()]

stop.cummax() is False before the first True and True from then on, so ~stop.cummax() selects everything strictly before the condition first appears. To include the triggering row use df_GPS.loc[:stop.idxmax()] (guard with stop.any(), since idxmax returns 0 when the condition never occurs). If you want query syntax, pre-compute the flag: df_GPS.assign(stop=stop.cummax()).query('~stop'). The same trick generalizes with stop.cumsum().eq(0), and works for any combination of conditions on the speed columns.

Reinstalling VS Code doesn't reset extensions or settings (they live in your user profile), so your environment still differs from your colleagues'. Usual causes when breakpoints in an imported module stop binding: 1) The debugger runs a different copy of cn.py than the file you set breakpoints in. Check under the debugger: from src import cn; print(cn.__file__). Shadowing by an installed package with the same name, a stale copy elsewhere on sys.path, or launching from a different folder/cwd all cause this. 2) Stale bytecode — delete all __pycache__ folders. 3) If the module resolves outside the workspace (e.g. site-packages), set "justMyCode": false in launch.json. 4) A broken auto-update of the Python / Python Debugger (debugpy) extension — a sudden overnight breakage strongly suggests this; update or roll back the extension version. 5) Make sure you use Start Debugging with the correct launch config, not Run Without Debugging. Checking cn.__file__ usually pinpoints the problem immediately.

The bars aren't summed, they're stacked: Vega-Lite groups rows sharing the same x value and stacks the bars, which looks like 20+15=35. The idiomatic fix in Altair 5 is the xOffset channel: keep 'a' on the x axis (so labels come from 'a') and offset duplicate rows by a unique field such as the index:

alt.Chart(source.reset_index()).mark_bar().encode(
    x='a:N',
    xOffset='index:O',
    y='b:Q'
)

This draws 4 bars, the two B rows side by side under a single 'B' label — no fake combined column or labelExpr trickery needed. If instead you want each bar at its own tick in original row order (exactly like df.plot(kind='bar')), your combined-column + labelExpr workaround is the practical route, but for distinct data points with the same category, xOffset (grouped/dodged bars) is the proper Altair solution. Setting alt.Y('b', stack=None) only overlays the bars, hiding the smaller one, so prefer xOffset.

Your build is fine — newer OpenCV interprets the arguments differently. np.uint8([250]) is a 1-D single-element array, and OpenCV 4.12 treats such an argument as a Scalar (a 4-tuple of doubles, like a BGRA color), not a 1x1 image. Scalar arithmetic is done in double precision with no saturation, so you get (250+10, 0, 0, 0) → [[260.],[0.],[0.],[0.]] with dtype float64. The documentation example predates this behavior change, when the same call produced a 1x1 uint8 Mat and saturated to 255. To reproduce the documented behavior, pass real 2-D arrays (images):

x = np.uint8([[250]])
y = np.uint8([[10]])
print(cv.add(x, y))   # [[255]]

(or np.full((1,1), 250, np.uint8)). With proper uint8 arrays cv.add saturates at 255 while NumPy's x+y wraps modulo 256 (gives 4). Don't cast the float64 result afterwards: astype(np.uint8) wraps 260 to 4, which is exactly the modulo behavior you're trying to avoid.

A manager Pool proxy doesn't survive being shipped to another process the way you're using it. When the PoolProxy is unpickled inside the spawned child, its _manager attribute is set to None (only the connection token is kept). apply_async needs self._manager._registry to construct the AsyncResult proxy, hence AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute '_registry'. Manager pools effectively only support proxy-returning methods from the process that owns the manager. Practical rule: allocate the pool in the process that submits the work.

def poolprocess():
    with mp.get_context('spawn').Pool() as pool:
        res = pool.apply_async(poolswimmer)
        res.wait()

if __name__ == '__main__':
    p = mp.Process(target=poolprocess)
    p.start(); p.join()

A plain multiprocessing.Pool can't be pickled at all — by design, pools are owned by one process. Alternatively drop the intermediate process and create the Pool in __main__, submitting all CPU-bound jobs from there (concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor works too). If several I/O driver processes each need workers, create a small pool inside each driver's target function.

Polars has a direct equivalent: is_first_distinct (called is_first in older versions), applied to a struct of the subset columns:

import polars as pl
df_pl = pl.from_pandas(df)

df_pl = df_pl.with_columns(
    pl.struct(['store', 'item', 'date'])
      .is_first_distinct()
      .cast(pl.Int64)
      .alias('Total_SKU_Count')
)

For subset ['store','item'] just change the struct fields. This marks the first occurrence of each unique combination with 1 and later duplicates with 0 — exactly (~df.duplicated(subset, keep='first')).astype(int) — and drops no rows.

A version-agnostic alternative is a window expression that numbers rows within each group and flags the first:

df_pl.with_columns(
    (pl.int_range(pl.len()).over(['store','item','date']) == 0)
      .cast(pl.Int64)
      .alias('Total_SKU_Count')
)

(use pl.arange(0, pl.count()).over(...) in older Polars). Both rely on the current row order to define "first", matching pandas' keep='first' semantics.

Several bugs combine here. 1) In the except block you assign errror (typo, three r's), so error never becomes "yes", and the bare except hides the real exception. 2) The exception itself is almost certainly type=student — student is an undefined name; you mean type='student' (a string). Temporarily remove the try/except (or use except Exception as e and log/print e) to see the real traceback. 3) Template syntax: {% if user error == "no" %} is invalid — it must be {% if error == "no" %}; and {% if error =="yes"} is missing the closing %}. 4) window.location("...") is not a function — use window.location.href = "{% url 'user_login' %}";. 5) Because you read request.FILES['images'], the form tag needs enctype="multipart/form-data", or the POST raises KeyError. Better practice: on success use Django's messages framework (messages.success(request, 'Signed up successfully')) and return redirect('user_login') instead of injecting alert() scripts.

Yes, this is expected Snakemake behavior. use rule ... with: does not merge directives — any directive you specify replaces the inherited rule's directive entirely. params is one directive, so redefining it with only rebin=20 throws away variable, giving AttributeError: 'Params' object has no attribute 'variable'. Options: 1) Repeat all params in the override:

use rule analysis from analysis as run_analysis with:
    params:
        variable="SvB",
        rebin=20

2) Don't override params at all — make the base rule read config with defaults, so importing workflows only set config values (you already pass config: config to the module):

params:
    variable=lambda wc: config.get("variable", "SvB"),
    rebin=lambda wc: config.get("rebin", 10)

Option 2 is the usual pattern for reusable module rules: one canonical params definition driven by config, and no params section in the use rule statement.

InvalidCiphertextException from KMS in the DAS pipeline almost always means the decrypt parameters don't match how RDS encrypted the data key. Check in order: 1) Encryption context. The per-record data key must be decrypted with exactly EncryptionContext={'aws:rds:dbc-id': <cluster resource id>} for Aurora clusters (or 'aws:rds:db-id': <DbiResourceId> for instance-level streams). If the sample's RESOURCE_ID variable holds the cluster name or ARN instead of the resource id (which looks like cluster-ABCD1234...), KMS raises InvalidCiphertextException. Get it via aws rds describe-db-clusters --query 'DBClusters[].DbClusterResourceId'. 2) Decrypt the right thing: base64-decode the Kinesis record, JSON-parse it, KMS-decrypt only the key field (the enveloped data key), then decrypt databaseActivityEvents with the AWS Encryption SDK using that plaintext key. Passing the payload itself to kms.decrypt also produces this error. 3) Use the same KMS key (the activity stream's KmsKeyId) in the same region, with kms:Decrypt granted to the Lambda role. Point 1 is the most common culprit with this exact aws-samples function.

Your pattern (lifespan + app.state + small dependency) is the standard, recommended approach. Alternatives: 1) Lifespan state: yield {'session': session} from lifespan and read request.state.session — same idea without touching app.state. 2) Module-level singleton created in lifespan and imported where needed — simple, but hides the dependency and is harder to override in tests. 3) Per-request client via a yielding dependency (async with httpx.AsyncClient() as c: yield c) — cleanest isolation but loses connection pooling/keep-alive, the main reason for sharing. 4) A DI container (e.g. dependency-injector) for larger apps. Caveats of the shared client: set limits and timeouts explicitly, since they apply globally; never mutate shared state per request — response cookies persist on the client and can leak between users, so avoid cookie-based auth on a shared client; base_url/headers are global; requests in flight at shutdown fail once lifespan closes it. For tests, use app.dependency_overrides to swap get_session for a client with httpx.MockTransport.

Two moviepy gotchas cause this. 1) In the resize fx, if height is given, width is ignored (height takes precedence and aspect ratio is preserved), so your image became 2570x960 instead of 1080x960. Pass the target size as a tuple: image_clip = image_clip.resize((1080, 960)) (i.e. newsize=(1080, 960)). 2) CompositeVideoClip takes its canvas size from the first clip unless you pass size=. Your first clip was the 2570x960 image, hence the 2570x960 output with everything else off-canvas/blank. Be explicit:

final = CompositeVideoClip([image_clip, video_clip, text_clip], size=(1080, 1920))

Then position the pieces: image_clip.set_position((0, 0)), video_clip.set_position((0, 960)) for the bottom half, text_clip.set_position('center'). Also set the composite duration (final = final.set_duration(video_clip.duration)) and write with an explicit fps, e.g. final.write_videofile(output_path, fps=video_clip.fps) — composites whose first clip is an ImageClip can otherwise yield an unplayable file. With the tuple resize and size=(1080,1920) you get the intended 1080x1920 layout.
